newsitem.title: FRANCE: France hopes to advance NATO-Russia talks.
newsitem.headline: France hopes to advance NATO-Russia talks.

text.p: France hopes to boost negotiations on a new relationship between Russia and NATO and may offer to host the signing ceremony when Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov visits Paris this week, diplomats said on Monday.

Primakov, due to have a fresh round of talks with NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana in Moscow on April 15, is to meet Foreign Minister Herve de Charette on Tuesday and President Jacques Chirac on Wednesday.
The trip is seen in Moscow as part of Primakov's efforts to negotiate conditions for the planned eastward expansion of NATO that would inflict minimal damage and humiliation on Russia.

The talks are also expected to cover Moscow's bid for membership of the Paris club of creditor nations and last week's union treaty between Russia and Belarus, which France said must take account the wishes of the people of both countries.

The 16-nation western defence alliance is expected to invite at least three of Moscow's former Warsaw Pact allies -- Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic -- to begin NATO membership negotiations at a summit in Madrid in July.

France did not comment when a Russian news agency reported recently that Paris might host a mini-summit at which a document enshrining a new, cooperative NATO-Russia relationship would be ceremonially signed.

But Western diplomats and NATO officials said they believed Chirac was keen to have the pact signed in Paris in late May to show that France was playing a major role in a reformed NATO and help ease a solution to his dispute with the United States over the alliance's southern command.

"It would be a neat way to give France a visible role and tie up a compromise on the southern command leading to a French return to NATO's military structure. But it's certainly not a done deal at this stage," one diplomat said.

He said Paris would first have to accept a compromise under which the question of whether to hand the U.S.-held Naples command, which controls the Mediterranean, over to a European officer would be postponed for several years.

NATO sources say detailed negotiations between the alliance and Russia have advanced since Presidents Bill Clinton and Boris Yeltsin agreed in Helsinki last month to build a partnership meant to ease Moscow's hostility to NATO's eastward enlargement.

NATO's Brussels headquarters has exchanged draft documents with Moscow and the sources said there was substantial progress on four of the five main points: a preamble on the framework for European security, principles of cooperation, a NATO-Russia joint council and the main areas of cooperation.
The main outstanding difference concerned limits on NATO infrastructure on the territory of new member states which were former communist allies of the Soviet Union, they said.
A NATO source said Clinton and Yeltsin set a tentative date of May 27 for a signing ceremony "somewhere in Europe".
Clinton, whose travel has been restricted by a knee injury, is due to be in The Hague the following day for a summit between the United States and the European Union.

Russian foreign ministry officials said Moscow was watching closely the dispute between Paris and Washington over who commands NATO's southern flank as a sign of apparent discontent among European countries with U.S. domination of the alliance.

Chirac is probably the NATO leader most sympathetic to Russia's concerns and is particularly understanding of its determination that former Soviet republics -- notably the three Baltic republics -- should not joint the western alliance.
The French leader has said it is vital not to humiliate Russia, a great nation, at a time when it appears weak.
